====United Kingdom====
[[File:Pimlico accumulator tower 1.jpg|thumb|right|District heating accumulator tower and workshops on the [[Churchill Gardens]] Estate, [[Pimlico]], London. This plant once used waste heat piped from [[Battersea Power Station]] on the other side of the [[River Thames]]. (January 2006)]]
In the United Kingdom, district heating became popular after World War II, but on a restricted scale, to heat the large residential estates that replaced dwellings destroyed by the [[The Blitz|Blitz]]. In 2013 there were 1,765 district heating schemes, with 920 based in London alone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Summary evidence on District Heating Networks in the UK|url= https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/212565/summary_evidence_district_heating_networks_uk.pdf |publisher=DECC}}</ref> In total around 210,000 homes and 1,700 businesses are supplied by heat networks in the UK.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Future of Heating: Meeting the Challenge|url= https://www.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/190149/16_04-DECC-The_Future_of_Heating_Accessible-10.pdf |publisher=DECC}}</ref>

The [[Pimlico District Heating Undertaking]] (PDHU) in London first became operational in 1950 and continues to expand to this day. The PDHU once relied on waste heat from the now-disused [[Battersea Power Station]] on the south side of the [[River Thames]]. It is still in operation; the water is now heated locally by a new energy centre which incorporates 3.1 [[MWe]] / 4.0 [[MWth]] of gas fired CHP engines and 3 × 8 MW gas-fired boilers.

One of the United Kingdom's largest district heating schemes is EnviroEnergy in [[Nottingham]]. The plant, initially built by [[Boots (company)|Boots]], is now used to heat 4,600 homes, and a wide variety of business premises, including the [[Nottingham Royal Concert Hall|Concert Hall]], the [[Motorpoint Arena Nottingham|Nottingham Arena]], the Victoria Baths, the [[Broadmarsh|Broadmarsh Shopping Centre]], the [[Victoria Centre]], and others. The heat source is a [[waste-to-energy]] incinerator.

[[Sheffield]]'s district heating network was established in 1988 and is still expanding today. It saves an equivalent 21,000 plus tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> each year when compared to conventional sources of energy – electricity from the national grid and heat generated by individual boilers. There are currently over 140 buildings connected to the district heating network. These include city landmarks such as the [[Sheffield City Hall]], the [[Lyceum Theatre, Sheffield|Lyceum Theatre]], the [[University of Sheffield]], [[Sheffield Hallam University]], hospitals, shops, offices and leisure facilities plus 2,800 homes. More than 44 km of underground pipes deliver energy which is generated at [[Sheffield Energy Recovery Facility]]. This converts 225,000 tonnes of waste into energy, producing up to 60 MWe of thermal energy and up to 19 MWe of electrical energy.

The [[Southampton District Energy Scheme]] was originally built to use just geothermal energy, but now also uses the heat from a gas-fired CHP generator. It supplies heating and [[district cooling]] to many large premises in the city, including the [[Westquay]] shopping centre, the De Vere Grand Harbour hotel, the [[Royal South Hants Hospital]], and several housing schemes. In the 1980s [[Southampton]] began to use combined heat and power district heating, taking advantage of geothermal heat "trapped" in the area. The geothermal heat provided by the well works in conjunction with the Combined Heat and Power scheme. Geothermal energy provides 15–20%, [[fuel oil]] 10%, and natural gas 70% of the total heat input for this scheme and the combined heat and power generators use conventional fuels to make electricity. "Waste heat" from this process is recovered for distribution through the 11 km mains network.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Geothermie district heating scheme Southampton United Kingdom|url=http://www.energie-cites.org/db/southampton_140_en.pdf|access-date=2007-01-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927205633/http://www.energie-cites.org/db/southampton_140_en.pdf|archive-date=2007-09-27}} 080304 energie-cites.org</ref>

Scotland has several district heating systems. The first in the UK was installed at [[Aviemore]], and others followed at [[Lochgilphead]], [[Fort William, Scotland|Fort William]] and Forfar. [[Lerwick District Heating and Energy Recovery Plant|Lerwick District Heating Scheme]] in Shetland is of note because it is one of the few schemes where a completely new system was added to a previously existing small town.

[[Association for Decentralised Energy|ADE]] has an online map of district heating installations in the UK.<ref>{{cite web |title=District Heating Installation Map |url=https://www.theade.co.uk/resources/district-heating-installation-map |publisher=ADE}}</ref> ADE estimates that 54 percent of energy used to produce electricity is being wasted via conventional power production, which relates to £9.5 billion ($US12.5 billion) per year.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/articles/2017/11/what-a-waste-the-big-problem-of-heat-loss-in-uk-cities.html |title=What a Waste! The Big Problem of Heat Loss in UK Cities|work=www.renewableenergyworld.com |first= Kirsty |last=Lambert |date=9 November 2017 |access-date=12 November 2017}}</ref>

In the United Kingdom, the Heat Network Technical Assurance Scheme (HNTAS) is a regulatory framework being developed to establish minimum technical standards and an assurance process for heat networks. The scheme, underpinned by powers in the Energy Act 2023, is intended to require compliant heat networks to demonstrate that they meet mandated technical requirements throughout their lifecycle, covering design, installation, operation, and performance monitoring. HNTAS includes a structured assessment and certification system, with draft technical specifications and procedures published by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to support implementation. It is designed to improve the reliability, efficiency, and transparency of heat networks, and will apply to networks ranging from small communal systems to larger district heating schemes. DMS can advise.<ref name="HNTAS1">{{cite web |title=Heat Network Technical Assurance Scheme (HNTAS) |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-networks-regulation-technical-standards/heat-network-technical-assurance-scheme-hntas |publisher=GOV.UK}}</ref><ref name="HNTAS2">{{cite web |title=Heat networks regulation: technical standards |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-networks-regulation-technical-standards |publisher=GOV.UK}}</ref>

===North America===
In North America, district heating systems fall into two general categories. Those that are owned by and serve the buildings of a single entity are considered institutional systems. All others fall into the commercial category.

{{As of|2013}}, approximately 2,500 district heating and cooling systems existed in the United States, in one form or another, with the majority providing heat.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=HPACEngineering|title=Why Is District Energy Not More Prevalent in the U.S.?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180326040957/https://www.hpac.com/heating/why-district-energy-not-more-prevalent-us|url=https://www.hpac.com/heating/why-district-energy-not-more-prevalent-us|archive-date=March 26, 2018|date=June 7, 2013|publisher=Informa}}</ref>
* [[Consolidated Edison]] of [[New York (state)|New York]] (Con Ed) operates the New York City steam system, the largest commercial district heating system in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/coned.html |title=Con Ed Steam |publisher=Energy.rochester.edu |access-date=2011-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070921191139/http://www.energy.rochester.edu/us/coned.html |archive-date=2007-09-21 }}</ref> The system has operated continuously since March 3, 1882, and serves [[Manhattan Island]] from the Battery through 96th Street.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.coned.com/history/steam.asp |title=A Brief History of Con Edison |publisher=Con Edison |access-date=2014-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151114152015/http://www.coned.com/history/steam.asp |archive-date=2015-11-14 }}</ref> In addition to providing space- and water-heating, steam from the system is used in numerous restaurants for food preparation, for process heat in laundries and dry cleaners, for steam sterilization, and to power [[Absorption refrigerator|absorption chiller]]s for [[air conditioning]]. On July 18, 2007, one person was killed and numerous others injured when a [[2007 New York City steam explosion|steam pipe exploded]] on 41st Street at Lexington.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/6905738.stm | work=BBC News | title=Explosion rocks central New York | date=July 19, 2007 | access-date=May 1, 2010}}</ref> On August 19, 1989, three people were killed in an [[Gramercy Park asbestos steam explosion|explosion in Gramercy Park]].<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/07/19/nyregion/19explode.html?ex=1342584000&en=c9164269910ddad6&ei=5124&partner=permalink&exprod=permalink | work=The New York Times | title=Steam Blast Jolts Midtown, Killing One | first=James | last=Barron | date=July 19, 2007 | access-date=May 1, 2010}}</ref>

====China====
In southern [[China]] (south of the [[Qinling–Huaihe Line]]), there are nearly no district heating systems. In northern China, district heating systems are common.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Guan Jin |first1=James |title=District Energy in China |url=https://www.euroheat.org/knowledge-hub/district-energy-china/ |website=Euroheat&Power |access-date=21 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Jingjing |last2=Di Lucia |first2=Lorenzo |title=A transition perspective on alternatives to coal in Chinese district heating |journal=International Journal of Sustainable Energy Planning and Management |date=23 September 2015 |volume=6 |doi=10.5278/ijsepm.2015.6.5}} {{open access}}</ref> Most district heating systems are just for heating by burning [[Anthracite|hard coal]] instead of [[Cogeneration|CHP]]. Since [[air pollution in China]] has become quite serious, many cities gradually are now using natural gas rather than coal in district heating system. There is also some amount of geothermal heating<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tester |first1=Jeff |title=U.S. lagging in geothermal energy as China and others pull ahead |url=https://www.axios.com/us-lagging-in-geothermal-energy-as-china-and-others-pull-ahead-ea7ce800-df9b-431c-896c-8b1ab4bb9da2.html |website=Axios |date=17 July 2018 |access-date=21 February 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hallsson |first1=Hallur |title=The Icelandic geothermal model is changing China |url=https://icelandictimes.com/the-icelandic-geothermal-model-is-changing-china/ |website=Icelandic Times |access-date=21 February 2020 |date=1 October 2019}}</ref> and sea heat pump systems.<ref name="SeawaterHeatPumps">{{cite journal |author1=Chang Su |author2=Hatef Madani |author3= Hua Liu|author4= Ruzhu Wang |author5= Björn Palm |year=2020 |title=Seawater heat pumps in China, a spatial analysis |journal=Energy Conversion and Management |volume=203 |page=112440 |article-number=112240 |doi=10.1016/j.enconman.2019.112240|bibcode=2020ECM...20312240S |s2cid=209702976 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:kth:diva-266164 }}</ref>

extract:
District heating (also known as heat networks) is a system for distributing heat generated in a centralized location through a system of insulated pipes for residential and commercial heating requirements such as space heating and water heating. The heat is often obtained from a cogeneration plant burning fossil fuels or biomass, but heat-only boiler stations, geothermal heating, heat pumps and central solar heating are also used, as well as heat waste from factories and nuclear power electricity generation. District heating plants can provide higher efficiencies and better pollution control than localized boilers. According to some research, district heating with combined heat and power (CHPDH) is the cheapest method of cutting carbon emissions, and has one of the lowest carbon footprints of all fossil generation plants.
District heating is ranked number 27 in Project Drawdown's 100 solutions to global warming.
